body:
Sequencing answers a different question from PCR

DNA sequencing determines the exact order of the bases A, T, G and C in a DNA segment. Knowing that a target DNA region is present is not the same as knowing its sequence. PCR is useful when more copies of a selected target are needed; sequencing is useful when the order of the letters, or a change in that order, must be identified.

For example, a test that only detects a particular gene may report that it is present. Sequencing a region of that gene can reveal whether its bases match a comparison sequence or contain a variation. Some variations affect a protein's function; others have no known harmful effect. A sequence difference is therefore not automatically a diagnosis.

What is sequenced: one region or a whole genome?

Targeted sequencing reads a chosen gene or DNA region. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) aims to determine the DNA sequence across an organism's complete genome, not just its protein-coding genes. The human genome includes a large amount of DNA outside protein-coding regions; whole-genome data may therefore reveal information that a single-gene test would miss.

Several sequencing technologies exist. Sanger sequencing, associated with Frederick Sanger, is a well-established method for reading selected DNA sequences. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) allows very many DNA fragments to be read in parallel, making larger sequencing studies possible. These names describe ways of obtaining sequence information, not different forms of DNA or ways to edit genes.

A single-base change can matter

Consider 2 invented DNA strings used only to illustrate comparison: ATGCCTA and ATACCTA. They differ at the 3rd base, where G has become A. Sequencing can reveal such a substitution; its biological importance cannot be inferred from these letters alone. The same principle allows researchers to compare an individual's DNA with a reference, or different samples of a pathogen with one another.

What sequence information is used for

  • Diagnosis: identifying relevant sequence changes in an inherited disorder, when the test and clinical evidence support that interpretation.
  • Infectious disease surveillance: comparing pathogen genomes to recognise genetic variants and investigate how they are related.
  • Agriculture: comparing crop varieties, detecting genetic differences relevant to breeding and identifying organisms affecting plants.

DNA fingerprinting is a related but distinct idea: it compares informative variable DNA regions or patterns to help identify individuals or biological relationships. It need not involve reading the entire genome. Neither fingerprinting nor DNA sequencing is the same as changing DNA through genetic engineering.

The DNA sequence shows what bases are present. It does not, by itself, show exactly when a gene is active, how much protein it produces, whether a detected mutation is harmful or whether a person certainly has a disease.

Prelims focus

  • DNA sequencing determines the order of A, T, G and C bases.
  • PCR amplifies a DNA region; sequencing reads the bases of a DNA region.
  • Whole-genome sequencing covers the genome, not only protein-coding genes.
  • Sanger sequencing and next-generation sequencing are named sequencing approaches.
  • Sequence comparison can identify genetic variants.
  • Trap: A detected sequence variant is not necessarily disease-causing.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class 12, “Molecular Basis of Inheritance”, §§6.9–6.10 (GPSC Books vol. 35, PDF pp. 121–126); NHGRI, “DNA Sequencing Fact Sheet”, sections “What is DNA sequencing?” and “How new is DNA sequencing?”, and “A Brief Guide to Genomics”, section “What is DNA sequencing?” (consulted 5 November 2026).]

title: DNA sequencing: reading the order of genetic letters

body:
Different questions require different DNA methods

DNA-based biotechnology is useful because it can detect selected genetic material, read its base sequence or use genes to produce a desired biological product. The correct method depends on the question, not simply on whether DNA is involved.

  • Presence of a pathogen's DNA or RNA: PCR or RT-PCR can detect an appropriate target even when only a small amount is present.
  • Identity of a genetic variant: sequencing can show the exact bases in a selected region or across a genome.
  • Production of a therapeutic protein: recombinant DNA technology can enable suitable host cells to manufacture the product, as in recombinant human insulin.
  • Identification or improvement of crops: genetic markers and sequencing help distinguish varieties or traits; recombinant DNA can introduce a selected trait into a crop.

Biotechnology in Indian agriculture

Bt cotton is a direct example of an introduced gene producing a useful agricultural trait. It uses gene information originating from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis so that cotton plants make particular insecticidal proteins. These proteins provide protection against susceptible bollworm pests, rather than general protection against every agricultural threat.

India approved commercial cultivation of Bt cotton in 2002. A Union agriculture ministry statement dated 6 August 2024 identified Bt cotton as the only genetically modified crop approved for commercial cultivation at the time of that statement. This dated approval status should not be confused with the many GM crops used or studied elsewhere, or with a permanent rule that could never change. Ordinary crop breeding and DNA-marker-based selection are also biotechnology applications; a crop selected with DNA markers is not automatically genetically modified.

GenomeIndia: studying the genetic diversity of India

The GenomeIndia Project is supported by the Department of Biotechnology (DBT), Government of India. Its purpose is to map genetic variation among India's diverse population groups and support future research on inherited conditions and health. A government status release dated 30 April 2025 reported that whole-genome sequencing data had been completed for more than 10,000 individuals. This is a dated project milestone, not a count of people clinically diagnosed with disease or a claim that every Indian has been sequenced.

Gujarat Biotechnology Research Centre

The Government of Gujarat established the Gujarat Biotechnology Research Centre (GBRC) in 2017 under its Department of Science and Technology. Located in Gandhinagar, GBRC works in areas that include genomics, molecular diagnostics and agricultural biotechnology. Its published services include DNA sequencing, genetic-marker analysis, gene-expression studies and transgene testing in crops. The Government of Gujarat's institutional profile, last updated 27 October 2026, also lists GBRC's participation in GenomeIndia and the Indian SARS-CoV-2 Genomics Consortium (INSACOG) for genomic surveillance.

Linking the methods: If a clinic seeks evidence of a particular virus, a suitable nucleic-acid amplification test can help detect it. If researchers must compare the genetic differences among virus samples, they need sequence information. If a manufacturer wants cells to produce human insulin, the central technique is recombinant DNA technology. The shared foundation is DNA or RNA, but the output differs in each case.

Prelims focus

  • Bt cotton contains insect-resistance gene information from Bacillus thuringiensis.
  • Bt cotton was approved for commercial cultivation in India in 2002.
  • GenomeIndia is a DBT-supported project to study India's genetic variation.
  • DBT reported sequencing data for more than 10,000 individuals on 30 April 2025.
  • GBRC was established in 2017 and is based in Gandhinagar.
  • Trap: A gene-detection test, sequencing study and genetically engineered product answer different biological questions.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class 12, “Biotechnology and its Applications”, §§12.1–12.2 (GPSC Books vol. 35, PDF pp. 232–237); Government of India, Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, “Cultivation of Genetically Modified crops” (6 August 2024); Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Science and Technology, “GenomeIndia” (30 April 2025); Government of Gujarat, Department of Science and Technology, “Gujarat Biotechnology Research Centre”, “Overview”, “Important Projects and Programs” and “Technologies Developed” (webpage last updated 27 October 2026); GBRC, “Facilities and Services: Services” (consulted 5 November 2026).]
